G. |last7=Hetherington |first7=Alistair M. |last8=Beneragama |first8=Chalinda K. |date=July 2021 |title="Ceylon cinnamon": Much more than just a spice |journal=Plants, People, Planet |language=en |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=319–336 |doi=10.1002/ppp3.10192 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021PlPP....3..319S |s2cid=234875442 |issn=2572-2611|hdl=1983/3e7af5bd-c4fd-4939-abe6-d908da1dbf4a |hdl-access=free }}</ref>), also known as '''true cinnamon''' or '''Ceylon cinnamon''', is a small [[evergreen]] [[tree]] belonging to the family [[Lauraceae]], native to [[Sri Lanka]].<ref name=EB>{{cite book |title=Encyclopædia Britannica |year=2008 |chapter=Cinnamon |quote=(species Cinnamomum zeylanicum), bushy evergreen tree of the laurel family ([[Lauraceae]]) native to Bangladesh, Sri Lanka (Ceylon), the neighboring Malabar coast of India, and Myanmar (Burma), and also cultivated in South America and the West Indies for the spice consisting of its dried inner bark. The bark is widely used as a [[spice]] due to its distinct flavour.}}</ref> The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice [[cinnamon]],<ref name="Suriyagoda" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Medicinal Spices Exhibit - UCLA Biomedical Library: History & Special Collections |url=https://unitproj.library.ucla.edu/biomed/spice/index.cfm?displayID=5 |access-date=2023-06-20 |website=unitproj.library.ucla.edu}}</ref> though this name has also been used for ''[[Cinnamomum cassia|C. cassia]]'' (cassia) as well.<ref name="Suriyagoda"/>

==Description==
''Cinnamomum verum'' is an evergreen tree growing to {{convert|10–15|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are [[ovate (leaf)|ovate]]-oblong in shape and {{convert|7–18|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The [[flower]]s, which are arranged in [[panicle]]s, are greenish and have a distinct scent. The [[fruit]] is a purple 1 cm (0.5 in) [[drupe]] containing a single [[seed]].<ref>[https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cinnamomum+verum Cinnamomum verum Cinnamon, Ceylon Cinnamon Tree PFAF Plant Database]</ref>

==Cultivation==
The old botanical synonym for the tree, ''Cinnamomum zeylanicum'', is derived from [[Sri Lanka]]'s former name, Ceylon.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/shared/spl/hi/picture_gallery/07/south_asia_sri_lanka0s_spice_of_life/html/1.stm | title=In pictures: Sri Lanka's spice of life| work=BBC News}}</ref> Sri Lanka still produces 80–90% of the world's supply of ''C. verum'';<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://druera.com/blogs/ceylon-cinnamon-basics/why-ceylon-cinnamon-10x-more-expensive-than-cassia|title=Why Ceylon Cinnamon 10x More Expensive than Cassia |date=2025-04-21|website=Druera Ceylon Cinnamon}}</ref> it is also cultivated on a commercial scale in the [[Seychelles]], [[Madagascar]] and [[Tanzania]].<ref name=fao93>{{cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/x5326e/x5326e07.htm |title=International trade in non-wood forest products: An overview |last=Iqbal |first=Mohammed |year=1993 |work= FO: Misc/93/11 – Working Paper |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|access-date=12 November 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.intracen.org/news/Upgrading-cinnamon-in-Tanzania/ |title=Upgrading cinnamon in Tanzania |work=ITC News |date=26 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220113051519/https://www.intracen.org/news/Upgrading-cinnamon-in-Tanzania/ |archive-date=2022-01-13}}</ref>

On [[Borneo]], ''Cinnamomum verum'' is cultivated at low elevations in [[Sarawak]] ([[Kuching District]]), [[Sabah]] (Keningau and Sandakan districts), and [[Kalimantan]].<ref name = Soh>{{cite journal | doi = 10.3767/000651911X615168 | title = Taxonomic revision of ''Cinnamomum'' (''Lauraceae'') in Borneo | date = 2011 | last1 = Wuu-Kuang | first1 = Soh | journal = Blumea - Biodiversity, Evolution and Biogeography of Plants | volume = 56 | issue = 3 | pages = 241–264 | bibcode = 2011Blume..56..241W | doi-access = free }}</ref>

There are several different [[cultivar]]s of ''Cinnamomum verum'' based on the taste of bark:<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.exportagridept.gov.lk/web/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=128&Itemid=159&lang=en |title=Cinnamon |location=Sri Lanka |publisher=Department of Export Agriculture |access-date=2015-10-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170428042959/http://www.exportagridept.gov.lk/web/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=128&Itemid=159&lang=en |archive-date=2017-04-28 }}</ref>

*  Weli Kurundu - Coarse
*  Thiththa Kurundu - Bitter

==Processing==
{{citations needed|section|date=March 2025}}
In cultivation, the trees are grown as leafy bushes, usually reaching a maximum of {{cvt|3|m|ft|0}} in height. They are first harvested at 3 years old and continue producing well for 40–50 years. Small side branches, {{cvt|1.5|–|5|cm}} in diameter, are removed from the trees. The outer bark is removed and processed into [[mulch]]. The twigs, leaves and berries (seeds) are crushed to make cinnamon oil, a less valuable byproduct. The inner bark of the branches is loosened by being rubbed with a brass rod. The bark is then split with a brass or stainless steel knife and peeled off as intact as possible. Long, full 'quills' of cinnamon are more valuable than broken pieces. These quills are then dried over several days in the shade, then in darkness. All this work is done by hand by experienced workers; this is the most expensive part of producing cinnamon spice. Finally, the dried bark is cut into sticks or ground into powder for sale to consumers.

==Grading==
{{See also|Food grading}}{{Unreferenced section|date=October 2025}}
The Sri Lankan grading system divides the cinnamon quills into four groups:
* Alba, less than {{cvt|6|mm}} in diameter
* Continental, less than {{cvt|16|mm}} in diameter
* Mexican, less than {{cvt|19|mm}} in diameter
* Hamburg, less than {{cvt|32|mm}} in diameter

These groups are further divided into specific grades. For example, Mexican is divided into M00000 special, M000000 and M0000, depending on quill diameter and number of quills per kilogram. Any pieces of bark less than {{cvt|106|mm}} long are sold as quillings. Featherings are the inner bark of twigs and twisted shoots. Chips are trimmings of quills, outer and inner bark that cannot be separated, or the bark of small twigs.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}}

== Medicinal uses ==
Cinnamon has a long history of use in [[traditional medicine]] as a digestive aid.<ref name="nccih">{{cite web|url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/cinnamon|title=Cinnamon|website=[[National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health]]|publisher=[[National Institutes of Health]]|date=2016|access-date=28 February 2017}}</ref>

Preliminary studies show that cinnamon could slow symptoms of [[Alzheimer's disease]] through the reduction of the oligomerisation of beta-amyloid.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0016564 | doi-access=free | title=Orally Administrated Cinnamon Extract Reduces β-Amyloid Oligomerization and Corrects Cognitive Impairment in Alzheimer's Disease Animal Models | year=2011 | last1=Frydman-Marom | first1=Anat | last2=Levin | first2=Aviad | last3=Farfara | first3=Dorit | last4=Benromano | first4=Tali | last5=Scherzer-Attali | first5=Roni | last6=Peled | first6=Sivan | last7=Vassar | first7=Robert | last8=Segal | first8=Daniel | last9=Gazit | first9=Ehud | last10=Frenkel | first10=Dan | last11=Ovadia | first11=Michael | journal=[[PLOS One]] | volume=6 | issue=1 | article-number=e16564 | pmid=21305046 | pmc=3030596 | bibcode=2011PLoSO...616564F }}</ref>
